questions.question_text: How many solutions does $x^{2}=100$ have, and what are they?

options.why: Took only the positive root, forgetting that $(-10)^{2}$ also gives $100$.
Halved $100$ instead of finding the number that multiplies by itself to give $100$.
Repeated the right-hand side as the solutions without undoing the square.

questions.solution_text:
$10\times 10=100$ and $(-10)\times (-10)=100$
$x=\pm 10$, so the equation has two solutions.

questions.question_text: Which one of these equations has exactly one solution?

options.why: Both $1$ and $-1$ square to give $1$, so this equation has two solutions, not one.
Confused having no solution with having one solution; nothing squares to give $-1$.
Counted only the positive root $8$, ignoring that $-8$ is also a solution.

questions.solution_text:
$0\times 0=0$, and no other number squares to give $0$.
$x^{2}=0$ has exactly one solution.

options.why: Square rooted $49$ and ignored the negative sign, but both $7$ and $-7$ square to give $+49$.
Assumed a negative right-hand side means the solution itself is negative.
Halved $49$ rather than testing whether a square can be negative at all.

questions.solution_text:
Squaring any number gives a positive result or zero.
The left-hand side can never equal $-49$.
There is no solution.

options.why: Applied the $\pm$ of the equation $x^{2}=25$ to the root sign, which stands for the positive root only.
Chose the negative root, but the root sign always gives the positive value.
Halved $25$ instead of finding the number that multiplies by itself to give $25$.

questions.solution_text:
$5\times 5=25$
The root sign stands for the positive root only.
$\sqrt{25}=5$

questions.question_text: Nina writes: “$x^{2}=196$, so $x=14$.” Which solution has she missed?

options.why: Made the right-hand side negative instead of taking the negative of the root.
Halved $196$ and made it negative instead of square rooting.
Halved the root $14$ rather than taking its opposite.

questions.solution_text:
$(-14)\times (-14)=196$
She has missed $x=-14$; the full answer is $x=\pm 14$.

questions.question_text: The side length $s$ cm of a square satisfies $s^{2}=121$. What is the side length?

options.why: Gave both solutions of the equation without rejecting the negative one, but a length cannot be negative.
Chose the negative solution, which cannot be a side length.
Halved $121$ instead of square rooting it.

questions.solution_text:
$s=\pm 11$
A side length cannot be negative, so $s=-11$ is rejected.
The side length is $11$ cm.

questions.question_text: The two solutions of $x^{2}=c$ are $x=9$ and $x=-9$. What is the value of $c$?

options.why: Doubled the solution instead of squaring it.
Assumed the negative solution requires a negative right-hand side.
Added the two solutions, $9+(-9)$, instead of substituting one into $x^{2}=c$.

questions.question_text: For which values of $c$ does the equation $x^{2}=c$ have exactly two solutions?

options.why: Counted $c=0$ as a two-solution case, but $x^{2}=0$ has the single solution $x=0$.
Assumed every equation of this form has two solutions, ignoring $c=0$ and negative values of $c$.
Linked the two solutions to the negative sign, but a negative right-hand side gives no solution at all.

questions.solution_text:
If $c>0$, both $\sqrt{c}$ and $-\sqrt{c}$ square to give $c$.
If $c=0$, only $x=0$ works, and if $c<0$ nothing works.
There are exactly two solutions when $c>0$.
